blocks.text: A carbon-fibre bicycle frame is more than twice as stiff as a steel one per kilogram, while a ceramic cutting tool can survive 3 GPa of compression but fracture at a tenth of that in tension. Both behaviours follow from how the materials are built from strong bonds and different phases.

blocks.markdown: **Ceramics** are compounds of metals and non-metals (oxides, carbides, nitrides) with ionic and covalent bonding. The bonds are strong, which makes ceramics stiff, hard and refractory. But the directional bonds, and the repulsion that arises when ions of like charge are forced to slide past each other, make dislocation motion very difficult at room temperature. Ceramics therefore show essentially no plastic deformation: they are brittle. Their strength is controlled by flaws.

blocks.title: Fracture toughness
blocks.text: The property $K_{Ic}$, in MPa$\sqrt{\mathrm m}$, is the critical stress-intensity factor at which a crack of length $a$ in a stressed body propagates unstably. Fracture occurs when $K=Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}$ reaches $K_{Ic}$, where $\sigma$ is the applied tensile stress and $Y$ is a geometry factor of order 1.

blocks.caption: Fracture stress falls as flaw size $a$ grows; $a$ in m, $K_{Ic}$ in Pa$\sqrt{\mathrm m}$.

blocks.title: Fracture stress of an alumina part
blocks.prompt: A technical alumina has a typical fracture toughness $K_{Ic}=4$ MPa$\sqrt{\mathrm m}$ and the largest surface flaw is 50 $\mu$m deep. Estimate the tensile stress to fracture, with $Y=1$.
blocks.answer: About 320 MPa in tension; the intrinsic compressive strength of alumina is many times higher.

blocks.markdown: **Tension versus compression.** A tensile stress pulls a crack open and concentrates stress at its tip. The stress there is amplified, and since the tip cannot blunt by plastic flow, the crack runs at a low average stress. A compressive stress closes the crack and does not concentrate stress in the same way, so cracks are far less likely to propagate. Compressive strengths of ceramics are often about ten times their tensile strengths, which is why ceramics are used in bearings, cutting tools and masonry-like loadings.

**Composites** combine two or more phases to get properties neither has alone. A fibre composite has strong, stiff fibres in a matrix (polymer, metal or ceramic) that holds them in place, transfers load and protects them. For loading *along* aligned continuous fibres, both constituents stretch equally (isostrain), so the composite stiffness is the volume-weighted average of the two, the **rule of mixtures**:

blocks.caption: $E_c$: longitudinal composite modulus; $V_f$, $V_m$: fibre and matrix volume fractions; $E_f$, $E_m$ their moduli. Assumes aligned continuous fibres and perfect bonding.

blocks.title: Glass-fibre/epoxy modulus and load sharing
blocks.prompt: A unidirectional glass/epoxy composite has $V_f=0.50$, with typical $E_f=72$ GPa and $E_m=3.0$ GPa. Find the longitudinal modulus and the fraction of axial load carried by the fibres.

steps.text: Load fraction in the fibres equals $V_fE_f/E_c$ (same strain, so load share is proportional to $VE$).

blocks.answer: $E_c=37.5$ GPa, and the fibres carry about 96 percent of the load although they are only 50 percent of the volume.

blocks.caption: Specific stiffness: stiffness per unit mass; GPa per Mg/m$^3$ is equivalent to MN m/kg.

blocks.title: Specific stiffness of carbon fibre against steel
blocks.prompt: A unidirectional carbon laminate has $V_f=0.6$, $E_f=230$ GPa, $E_m=3.5$ GPa, $\rho_f=1.8$ Mg/m$^3$ and $\rho_m=1.2$ Mg/m$^3$ (all typical). Compare its specific stiffness along the fibres with steel ($E=210$ GPa, $\rho=7.85$ Mg/m$^3$).
blocks.answer: The laminate is about 3.3 times stiffer per unit mass than steel along the fibres, even though its absolute modulus (139 GPa) is lower than that of steel (210 GPa).

blocks.caption: Specific stiffness of selected materials (typical values; composites in the fibre direction only).

items: Ceramic strength is flaw-limited and shows scatter, so design uses statistics and compressive loading.
Composites are anisotropic: the rule of mixtures is for loading along fibres; across the fibres, the isostress model $1/E_T=V_f/E_f+V_m/E_m$ gives a much lower value.
Specific stiffness $E/\rho$ is the right figure of merit where mass matters; a laminate's value is only reached along its fibre directions.
Quasi-isotropic laminates, with fibres in several directions, give a lower specific stiffness than the unidirectional value.

blocks.title: Direction matters
blocks.text: A unidirectional composite can be 15 times stiffer along the fibres than across them. Always state the loading direction when quoting a composite modulus.

points: Ceramics are strong in compression but weak in tension because flaws are closed by compression and opened by tension, and plastic flow cannot blunt cracks: $\sigma_f=K_{Ic}/(Y\sqrt{\pi a})$.
The longitudinal modulus of a fibre composite is $E_c=V_fE_f+V_mE_m$, with the fibres carrying most of the load.
Compare materials by specific stiffness $E/\rho$; a carbon-fibre laminate is roughly three times better than steel along the fibres.

questions.stem: Why are ceramics typically weak in tension even though their atomic bonds are very strong?

options.text: They contain small flaws, such as pores and microcracks, that concentrate stress and grow unstably because ceramics cannot yield plastically at the crack tip
Their bonds are weaker than those of metals
They contain mobile dislocations that move at low stress
They are always amorphous, so they have no strength

questions.correctOptionText: They contain small flaws, such as pores and microcracks, that concentrate stress and grow unstably because ceramics cannot yield plastically at the crack tip

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the strength is set by the largest flaw, not by the bond strength.
distractorRationale.b: Ionic and covalent bonds are generally as strong as or stronger than metallic bonds.
distractorRationale.c: Dislocation motion is very hard in ceramics at room temperature, which is why they are brittle.
distractorRationale.d: Many ceramics are crystalline; the problem is brittle fracture from flaws, not the lack of crystal structure.

questions.explanation: Fracture is controlled by the stress concentration at the tip of the worst flaw, $K=Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}$. Because ceramics cannot blunt the tip by plastic flow, the crack runs when $K$ reaches the fracture toughness, so the failure stress is far below the theoretical strength of the bonds.

questions.stem: Why is the compressive strength of a ceramic typically many times its tensile strength?

options.text: Under compression, flaws are pressed closed and do not grow unstably, so far higher stress is required to cause failure
Compression melts the ceramic locally and heals the cracks
Compression introduces dislocations that strengthen the ceramic
Ceramics have a higher modulus in compression than in tension

questions.correctOptionText: Under compression, flaws are pressed closed and do not grow unstably, so far higher stress is required to cause failure

distractorRationale.a: Correct: crack propagation is suppressed under compression.
distractorRationale.b: Compression does not melt the material.
distractorRationale.c: Plastic flow by dislocations is very limited in ceramics; the effect is on cracks, not dislocations.
distractorRationale.d: The modulus is nearly the same in both senses; the difference is in failure by crack growth.

questions.explanation: A tensile stress opens a flaw and concentrates stress at its tip, whereas a compressive stress closes it, so the crack cannot propagate simply. Compressive strengths of ceramics are therefore often around ten times their tensile strengths.

questions.stem: The longitudinal rule of mixtures, $E_c=V_fE_f+V_mE_m$, assumes that fibre and matrix are strained by the same amount along the fibre direction.
questions.explanation: The equation arises from an isostrain (Voigt) model in which fibres and matrix stretch together under a load along the fibres, so the composite stress is the volume-weighted sum of their stresses. Hence $E_c=V_fE_f+V_mE_m$, assuming perfect bonding and aligned continuous fibres.

questions.stem: A unidirectional carbon-fibre composite has a longitudinal modulus of about 139 GPa. How does its modulus perpendicular to the fibres compare, under an isostress model with $E_f=230$ GPa, $E_m=3.5$ GPa and $V_f=0.6$?

options.text: Much lower, about 8.6 GPa, because the soft matrix carries the load across the fibres
The same, 139 GPa, because the material is the same
Higher, about 230 GPa, because fibres are stiffest in every direction
About 3.5 GPa, exactly the matrix modulus

questions.correctOptionText: Much lower, about 8.6 GPa, because the soft matrix carries the load across the fibres

distractorRationale.b: The composite is strongly anisotropic; the modulus depends on direction relative to the fibres.
distractorRationale.c: Carbon fibres are stiff along their length; transverse loading is carried largely through the matrix.
distractorRationale.d: In the transverse direction, the fibres do add some stiffness, giving 8.6 GPa, so it is higher than the matrix alone.

questions.explanation: When loaded across the fibres, the stress is the same in fibre and matrix, so the strains add: $1/E_T=0.6/230+0.4/3.5=0.1169$ GPa$^{-1}$, giving $E_T=8.6$ GPa. The composite is therefore far stiffer along the fibres than across them, which is why fibre direction is designed to match the load path.

questions.stem: A unidirectional carbon-fibre/epoxy composite has a fibre volume fraction $V_f=0.55$. Take typical values $E_f=240$ GPa for the fibre and $E_m=3.2$ GPa for the epoxy. Use the rule of mixtures to calculate the longitudinal modulus in GPa.
questions.explanation: The matrix volume fraction is $V_m=1-0.55=0.45$. The rule of mixtures gives $E_c=V_fE_f+V_mE_m=0.55(240)+0.45(3.2)=132+1.44=133.4$ GPa. The fibres supply almost all of the stiffness.

questions.stem: A silicon nitride ceramic has an assumed fracture toughness $K_{Ic}=5.0$ MPa$\sqrt{\mathrm m}$. It contains a surface flaw of depth $a=40\ \mu$m. Taking the geometry factor $Y=1$, use $K_{Ic}=Y\sigma_f\sqrt{\pi a}$ to calculate the tensile fracture stress in MPa.
questions.explanation: Rearranging gives $\sigma_f=K_{Ic}/(Y\sqrt{\pi a})$. With $a=40\times10^{-6}$ m, $\sqrt{\pi a}=\sqrt{1.2566\times10^{-4}}=0.01121$ m$^{1/2}$, so $\sigma_f=5.0/0.01121=446$ MPa. Halving the flaw size would raise the failure stress by a factor of $\sqrt2$.

questions.stem: A unidirectional carbon-fibre laminate has $V_f=0.50$, $E_f=230$ GPa, $E_m=3.5$ GPa, fibre density 1.8 Mg/m$^3$ and matrix density 1.2 Mg/m$^3$. Steel has $E=210$ GPa and density 7.85 Mg/m$^3$. Calculate the ratio of the specific stiffness $E/\rho$ of the laminate (along the fibres) to that of steel (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: The longitudinal modulus is $0.5(230)+0.5(3.5)=116.75$ GPa and the density is $0.5(1.8)+0.5(1.2)=1.5$ Mg/m$^3$, so $E/\rho=77.8$ GPa per Mg/m$^3$. For steel, $210/7.85=26.8$. The ratio is $77.8/26.8=2.91$, so the laminate is about three times stiffer per unit mass in the fibre direction.

questions.stem: Which of the following candidate materials has the greatest specific stiffness $E/\rho$? Values are (E in GPa, density in Mg/m$^3$): A steel (210, 7.85); B aluminium alloy (70, 2.7); C glass-fibre composite (40, 1.9); D carbon-fibre composite along the fibres (140, 1.55).

options.text: D, with about 90 GPa per Mg/m$^3$
A, with about 27 GPa per Mg/m$^3$
B, with about 26 GPa per Mg/m$^3$
C, with about 21 GPa per Mg/m$^3$

questions.correctOptionText: D, with about 90 GPa per Mg/m$^3$

distractorRationale.b: Steel has the highest absolute modulus here but also the highest density; $210/7.85=26.8$.
distractorRationale.c: Aluminium is light but not much stiffer per unit mass than steel; $70/2.7=25.9$.
distractorRationale.d: The glass composite is the lowest here: $40/1.9=21$.

questions.explanation: Specific stiffness is $E/\rho$. The values are A 26.8, B 25.9, C 21.1 and D 90.3, so the carbon composite, with a moderate modulus but a low density, is clearly best in the fibre direction.

questions.stem: Explain why a ceramic is much weaker in tension than in compression, referring to the role of flaws, stress concentration and the absence of plastic deformation. Say how the strength depends on flaw size.
markingGuide: Ceramics contain pre-existing flaws (pores, microcracks, surface scratches) (1 mark)
Tensile stress opens a flaw and concentrates stress at the tip, with $K=Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}$ (2 marks)
Without dislocation motion the tip cannot blunt by plasticity, so the crack propagates when $K$ reaches $K_{Ic}$ (2 marks)
Strength falls as flaw size increases: $\sigma_f\propto1/\sqrt a$ (1 mark)
Under compression, flaws close and do not propagate in the same way, so strength is much higher, often ten times (2 marks)
questions.explanation: The strength of a ceramic is controlled by its worst flaw, not by the strength of its bonds. In tension the flaw is opened and grows unstably, whereas in compression it is closed.

questions.stem: A designer proposes a unidirectional carbon-fibre/epoxy beam with $V_f=0.65$, $E_f=240$ GPa and $E_m=3.0$ GPa. Calculate the longitudinal modulus using the rule of mixtures, calculate the fraction of the axial load carried by the fibres, and state two limitations of the rule of mixtures for this application.
markingGuide: Fibres carry about 99 percent of the load along the fibres (1 mark)
Limitation 1: valid only for loading along aligned continuous fibres with perfect bonding and equal strain (1 mark)
Limitation 2: modulus across the fibres is far lower (isostress, about 9 GPa), so a real beam needs off-axis plies or the load path must align with the fibres (2 marks)
Mentions that voids, fibre misalignment and imperfect bonding reduce the real value (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The rule of mixtures gives 157 GPa, with the fibres carrying 99 percent of the load because they are about 80 times stiffer than the matrix. The result applies only to the fibre direction and to ideal aligned fibres.
